sections.history: Sayavanam lies in the old Chola country on the northern bank of the Kaveri, a short distance from Poompuhar where the river reaches the sea. In the Tevaram hymns the place is called Tiruchaikkadu, and both Sambandar and Appar sang its Lord, which makes the temple a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name remembers a forest of saya grass, the korai reed of the Tamil country, that once covered the land. Tradition counts Sayavanam among the six Kaveri shrines held equal to Kasi, together with Tiruvaiyaru, Mayiladuthurai, Tiruvidaimarudur, Tiruvenkadu and Tiruvanchiyam. The present stone temple belongs to the medieval Chola period, with covered halls added later under the Marathas; local tradition credits the early Chola king Kochengat Chola with the first foundation.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, and above the sanctum rises a vimana that is described as octagonal in plan, a form less often seen in the Chola country. Within the sanctum stands the linga of Chayavaneswarar, and the goddess Kuyilinum Nanmozhi Ammai is honoured in her own shrine. The corridors and mandapas around the courtyard are largely the work of the later Maratha period. In the outer circuit are a shrine to the Nayanar saint Iyarpagai and his wife and a shrine to the three great Tevaram saints. Murugan is shown here with bow and arrow rather than the usual spear. The temple has two sacred waters, the Kaveri itself and the Airavata Teertham.
sections.legends: The great legend of Sayavanam concerns Indra, king of the gods. His mother Aditi had come down to earth to worship Chayavaneswarar and did not return. Searching for her, Indra found her at the temple and, resolved to uproot the whole temple and carry it away to his own realm on his white elephant Airavata. As the great beast began to dig in its tusks, the goddess spoke, and her voice was sweeter than the song of the nightingale; from this she is called Kuyilinum Nanmozhi Ammai, the mother whose words are sweeter than the kuyil's. Shiva then appeared before Indra and told him to give up his plan. The pool made where the elephant's tusks struck the earth is the Airavata Teertham.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the yearly cycle of Shaiva worship. Maha Shivaratri is observed with night-long worship, and the monthly Pradosham draws devotees at dusk, the hour dear to Shiva. The temple's utsavams follow the Tamil calendar, and the tradition of bathing in the Kaveri and the Airavata Teertham gives particular meaning to the days of festival. Specific festival dates and processions are not recorded in the sources we could verify, so please confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Sayavanam is a place for unhurried pilgrimage. Approach the east gate, pass beneath the gopuram, and stand before Chayavaneswarar before turning to the goddess whose name speaks of a sweet voice. Walk the outer circuit to see the shrines of Iyarpagai Nayanar and of the three saints, and look at Murugan with his bow. Many pilgrims visit the Airavata Teertham and pause to remember Indra's attempt and the Lord's gentle refusal. The temple lies only a few kilometres from Poompuhar and the sea, so it is easily visited together with the shrines of that coast, and the setting among fields and coconut groves has a calm of its own.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but not inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask the priest before photographing rituals or worshippers.
visit.gettingThere: Sayavanam is about 17 km from Sirkazhi and about 20 km from Mayiladuthurai, both of which have railway stations, and roughly 2 km from the coast and the Poompuhar estuary. Buses run along the Sirkazhi to Poompuhar road. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport, a long road journey away, so most pilgrims arrive by road or rail via Sirkazhi or Mayiladuthurai.
